candidates.attacker_control: Primary (TemplateManager): the raw NETCONF rpc-reply string returned by session.rpc(render(...)).get() is device-controlled XML that is handed straight to DocumentBuilder.parse(new InputSource(...)); a malicious or compromised managed device (or anyone able to inject into/replay the device's NETCONF session) controls it completely, including any XML prolog/DOCTYPE. Secondary (XmlString): same device-controlled replies are passed to prettifyXml() for logging from apps/configsync-netconf NetconfDeviceConfigSynchronizerProvider (lines 195/198) and ODTN/TAPI code; NetconfRpcParserUtil parses an arbitrary reply CharSequence passed by its caller.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) Devices are semi-trusted in SDN deployments and NETCONF in ONOS is normally carried over authenticated SSH, so the attacker model requires a malicious/compromised device or session injection - I could not prove an unauthenticated remote path. (2) The two sibling files show the project already knew and mitigated this class; that mitigation is simply absent from the sinks listed, which is consistent with an un-fixed code path rather than a deliberate exemption. (3) JAXB unmarshalling in NetconfRpcParserUtil uses the same reader, so entity resolution is not filtered elsewhere. (4) I verified no test or comment in the snapshot asserts DTD/entity handling, and that XmlConfigParser/NetconfAlarmTranslator are the only files containing the mitigation string.
candidates.impact: Controller-side XXE: reading files readable by the ONOS process (configuration, cluster metadata, keystores/credentials under the ONOS install) with out-of-band exfiltration via external DTD/parameter entities, blind SSRF against controller-reachable internal services, and denial of service through entity expansion (billion-laughs)/external fetches performed while a device event is being processed. Because ONOS typically runs with elevated privileges, file disclosure can expose credentials and enable lateral movement.
candidates.prerequisites: A managed NETCONF device (or an on-path/credential-holding attacker able to return crafted rpc-reply XML) for the templates-based drivers; ONOS must have the driver/behaviour active (e.g. Ciena Waveserver-Ai / C5162 / C5170 description, port-stats, link-discovery, port-admin behaviours all statically construct TemplateManager). For XmlString the XML must reach one of its logging call sites. No ONOS REST credentials are needed for the device-originated path.
candidates.root_cause: The remaining ONOS XML parsers that consume peer-supplied XML were never given the mitigation the project applies elsewhere: they instantiate a default parser (DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() / XMLInputFactory.newFactory()) with DTD processing, external general/parameter entities and external-DTD loading left at JDK defaults, and no XMLConstants.ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/ACCESS_EXTERNAL_SCHEMA restrictions, XIncludeAware=false or setExpandEntityReferences(false). The same repository already contains the project's intended countermeasure in two device-facing parsers — drivers/utilities/.../XmlConfigParser.loadXml (lines 54-69: DISALLOW_DTD_FEATURE + DISALLOW_EXTERNAL_DTD + setXIncludeAware(false) + setExpandEntityReferences(false), with the comment 'Disabling DTDs in order to avoid XXE xml-based attacks.') and providers/netconf/alarm/.../NetconfAlarmTranslator.createDocFromMessage (lines 98-108, identical pattern) — so the surviving sinks are a deviation from the project's own standard rather than an intentional design.
candidates.title: XXE: external-entity processing left enabled when ONOS parses XML received from managed devices (TemplateManager and sibling parsers)
candidates.trace: Device reply -> TemplateManager.InternalRequestDriver.doRequest (line 61) -> DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance().newDocumentBuilder().parse(new InputSource(CharSource.wrap(data).openStream())) (lines 62-64) with DTD/external entities enabled -> XPath evaluation of caller-supplied expressions (line 66) -> returned to driver behaviour, e.g. CienaWaveserverAiDeviceDescription.discoverDeviceDetails (lines 83-98) which feeds XPath text() results into DefaultDeviceDescription/annotations (serial-number, hw version, host-name) and thence to the ONOS device inventory surfaced by /onos/v1/devices and the GUI. An attacker device can therefore place an external entity (file://, http:// or parameter-entity/OOB-DTD construct) at a position the template's XPath selects, causing the controller to resolve it; blind SSRF/OOB exfiltration and entity-expansion DoS are also available. Parallel sinks: XmlString.prettyPrintXml (line 74 factory, 80-81/86-90 parse) and NetconfRpcParserUtil.parseRpcReply (line 59 factory with no XMLInputFactory.SUPPORT_DTD / IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES overrides, line 61 reader creation) exhibit the identical missing-hardening pattern; protocols/xmpp/.../XmlMerger.initDocBuilder (lines 57-62) and apps/odtn/api/.../YangToolUtil.toDocument (lines 196-205, 213-222) are the same shape but with weaker/CLI-only reachability.
candidates.unverified: Reachability of each sink at runtime was not executed or dynamically traced; I verified the call chains only by source text and the syntactic relation index (which has no data-flow or reachability semantics). Whether an exfiltrated value is reliably echoed back to the attacker (e.g. via the REST device inventory) depends on the driver/template XPath in use; blind SSRF/OOB-DTD exfiltration and DoS do not. The exact upstream fix commit for this case is not visible in the snapshot, so the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-611 Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference (blind file read / OOB exfiltration / SSRF / entity-expansion DoS)

coverage_summary: Files: the harness reports 10,611 files in the source root, 10,610 visible to me (1 excluded by a sensitive-name-or-path filter; binary-like files are refused/skipped). Relation index scope: 10,610 files seen, 8,074 Java files parsed, 1,448 omitted/unparsed, 15 parse errors, index_status=partial, and explicitly no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution or reachability analysis — all edges I used are syntactic candidates only. I inspected by source text: the REST/multipart upload surfaces (web/api resources: applications, configuration, ui preferences, diagnostics, docs, keys; apps/yang/web, apps/pce/pcerest, apps/vtn/vtnweb web.xml descriptors), the app archive lifecycle (core/common ApplicationArchive, DefaultApplicationId/ApplicationDescription), the YANG live compiler (apps/yang), XML parsing sites (drivers/utilities XmlConfigParser, providers/netconf/alarm NetconfAlarmTranslator, drivers/netconf TemplateManager, protocols/netconf/api NetconfRpcParserUtil, protocols/xmpp XmlMerger, utils/misc XmlString, apps/odtn YangToolUtil, apps/configsync-netconf), command-execution sites (web/api DiagnosticsWebResource, apps/cip ClusterIpManager, YangLiveCompilerManager), GUI/auth surfaces (web/gui UiExtensionManager, MainIndexResource, UiPreferencesWebResource, UiWebSocketServlet token generation), TLS helpers, and archive/zip handling. Not reviewed in depth: most driver implementations, the openstack/segmentrouting/vtn application logic, models/ and pipelines/, GUI2 Angular code, and non-Java assets; no tests, builds, scanners or requests were executed.
limitations: P1 index is partial (1,448 files omitted, 15 parse errors) and provides no control-flow/data-flow/reachability evidence; every chain above was re-verified in source text but not dynamically.
No code, tests or scanners were executed and no network requests were made, so all impact statements are source-based reasoning, not runtime confirmation.

The snapshot looks reduced/pruned relative to upstream ONOS: several app modules (e.g. apps/yang/web, apps/yang-gui, apps/artemis, apps/optical-rest, apps/powermanagement, apps/cord-support) have source trees but no pom.xml and no aggregator entry, so reachability claims for those modules (including the missing <security-constraint> lead) are unproven.

The upstream fix commit / test patch for this case is not present in the snapshot, so I cannot diff the vulnerable code against the fixed version; identification of the exact intended vulnerability therefore remains an inference.
1 file was hidden by the harness's sensitive-name/path filter; I could not determine what it is, and binary-like files were skipped by the read/search tools.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip-Slip / path injection in core/common ApplicationArchive: expandZippedApplication uses new File(appDir, entry.getName()) with only a name-based isTopLevel() gate (lines 351-372) and desc.name() from the uploaded app.xml as the base directory (expandPlainApplication line 428-434; saveApplication 191-215).
rejected_leads.reason: Real missing canonical-path validation, but the install surface (POST /onos/v1/applications, ApplicationsWebResource lines 95-144) is protected by the admin role (web/api WEB-INF/web.xml security-constraint), and an admin can already install arbitrary app code; written names are further constrained to *.jar/app.xml/features.xml, which heavily limits a useful target, so security impact is materially lower than the XXE lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip-Slip in apps/yang/src/main/java/org/onosproject/yang/impl/YangLiveCompilerManager.extractZipArchive (lines 117-131): entry names written under a temp dir with createParentDirs + Guava Files.write and no traversal check; modelId is then passed to bash scripts.
rejected_leads.reason: Strong code-level evidence but the reachable REST module apps/yang/web is not part of the build in this snapshot (no pom.xml and no aggregator entry), so the unauthenticated/authenticated HTTP path could not be established; CLI path requires shell access.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing <security-constraint> in apps/yang/web/src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/web.xml (unauthenticated compile/install of attacker YANG/ZIP) and the commented-out constraint with 'TODO: this should be uncommented' in apps/vtn/vtnweb/WEB-INF/web.xml (lines 22-33).
rejected_leads.reason: Deviation from the pattern used by ~20 sibling web.xml files is strong, but the yang web module is not built here and container-level auth cannot be exercised by a unit test, so I could not tie this to a verifiable failing test / reproducer.

rejected_leads.lead: Stored XSS via UI preferences: web/gui MainIndexResource.userPreferences embeds prefs.toString() unescaped in a <script> block (lines 127-133) and UiPreferencesWebResource PUT /ui/preferences/{user}/{pref} lets any authenticated caller write another user's preferences (lines 103-113).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible stored-XSS chain, but requires pref-write plus a victim GUI login and the escaping gap is a common-JSON-in-script issue; impact path less direct and no in-repo test target identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Trust-all TLS (CWE-295): RestDeviceProviderUtilities.enableSslCert (lines 40-74, with FIXME 'redo for security purposes'), OpenstackNodeUtil/OpenstackNetworkingUtil setDefaultSSLSocketFactory + allHostsValid, HttpSBControllerImpl trust-all TrustManager.
rejected_leads.reason: Deliberate, documented device-facing workarounds; enableSslCert has no callers in this snapshot, and no external attacker-controlled trigger into a privileged operation was traced, so it is a hardening/known-issue item rather than the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Kryo deserialization: org.onlab.util.KryoNamespace builds Kryo instances with kryo.setRegistrationRequired(registrationRequired) defaulting to false and StdInstantiatorStrategy (lines 453-464), used for cluster replication/primitive stores.
rejected_leads.reason: Would require an attacker able to inject cluster/Raft or primitive-store frames; no untrusted external entry point to those codecs was established from source in this review.

rejected_leads.lead: Insecure/plaintext handling: hardcoded Telnet password 'sdnip' in apps/artemis QuaggaBgpSpeakers (line 34) and InfluxDB password written to logs (InfluxDbMetricsConfig lines 137-141).
rejected_leads.reason: Credentials/hardening issues with no demonstrated attacker-controlled path to a security-impacting operation; both are configuration-adjacent and would not explain a test-verified vulnerability.

summary:
Snapshot = ONOS (onosproject/onos) at commit 033eff3b0546fe225c73, version 1.14.0-SNAPSHOT (approx. late-2018/early-2019, master), 10,610 model-visible files (10,611 on disk; 1 file hidden by the harness's sensitive-name filter; 1,448 index files unparsed). I traced attacker-controlled input through REST/multipart, NETCONF device replies, XMPP, config/GUI paths and packet paths, and compared each XML/archive/file-handling site against the hardening the project itself applies elsewhere.

Strongest, best-evidenced issue: XML external-entity (XXE) processing is left enabled in the remaining ONOS XML parsers that consume XML from a peer device/service (TemplateManager in drivers/netconf, XmlString in utils/misc, NetconfRpcParserUtil in protocols/netconf/api), while the very same codebase already contains the project's own mitigation for exactly this class in two sibling device-facing parsers (XmlConfigParser, NetconfAlarmTranslator: "Disabling DTDs in order to avoid XXE xml-based attacks"). These remaining parsers use a default DocumentBuilderFactory / XMLInputFactory with DTD and external-entity resolution enabled and no ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD restriction, so a managed device (or an on-path attacker able to inject into the device session) can make the controller resolve external entities — file read/OOB exfiltration/SSRF/entity-expansion DoS on the controller. Supporting details and alternate leads are listed below; nothing was executed and no runtime confirmation is claimed.

Separately noted but not chosen (see rejected_leads): Zip-Slip/path-injection in core/common ApplicationArchive (admin-only surface), Zip-Slip in YangLiveCompilerManager, missing <security-constraint> in apps/yang/web/WEB-INF/web.xml and the commented-out constraint in apps/vtn/vtnweb, stored-XSS via user preferences, trust-all TLS helpers, and default Kryo registration behavior.
